title: Resource curse

definition.text: The idea that countries rich in natural resources such as oil and minerals often see slower economic growth, weaker democracy or worse development than countries with fewer resources.

facts.text: Richard Auty first used the term 'resource curse' in 1993 for mineral-rich countries that grew more slowly than countries without plentiful resources.
The idea is older: in 1711 The Spectator observed that the most plentiful countries often had the poorest living.
A 1995 study by Jeffrey Sachs and Andrew Warner found a strong link between resource abundance and poor economic growth.
The IMF counts 51 countries as resource-rich, meaning at least 20% of exports or 20% of government revenue comes from nonrenewable resources; 29 of them are low or lower-middle income.
Oil and mineral prices swing widely, so governments that depend on them face volatile revenues that disrupt planning and debt payments.
Extraction tends to form an enclave with few links to the rest of the economy, and its high profits draw the best workers and investment away from other industries.
Countries whose economies are dominated by extraction tend to be less democratic and more corrupt; petroleum is the resource most consistently tied to weaker institutions.
Most experts think the curse is not universal or inevitable, but strikes certain kinds of countries under certain conditions.

contested_note: There is no academic consensus on whether resource abundance harms development; studies with empirical support reach contradictory findings.

definition.text: The large, sudden swings in government income that come from depending on natural resources whose prices fluctuate widely.

facts.text: Crude oil rose from $10 a barrel to $145 a barrel between 1998 and 2008, then fell by more than half to $60 in a few months.
In 2005, 99.3% of Angola's exports came from oil and diamonds alone.
Abrupt revenue changes often lead to broken contracts or cuts to social programmes, eroding the rule of law and public support.

definition.text: The tendency of a petrostate to start international conflicts or to be the target of them.

facts.text: Jeff Colgan's 2013 book popularised the term, finding that petrostates (10% or more of GDP from petroleum) are 250 percent more likely to start international conflicts than a typical country.
It remained unclear whether the same pattern holds for resources other than oil.

definition.text: The argument that heavy reliance on foreign aid can harm a country's development in the long run in the same way as the resource curse.

facts.text: Like resource revenue, aid is unearned income that can weaken politicians' accountability to citizens and reduce pressure to reform.
When aid is a major source of government revenue, it can reduce the incentive to build a tax system and respond to taxpayers.

title: Resource depletion

definition.text: The using up of a natural resource faster than it can be replaced.

facts.text: A resource's value depends on how much of it exists in nature and how costly it is to extract; under supply and demand, scarcer resources become more valuable.
Types of depletion include wetland and ecosystem degradation, soil erosion, aquifer depletion and overfishing.
Extraction of both renewable and non-renewable resources rose sharply with the Industrial Revolution, as new technology and economic growth raised demand.
Although rooted in colonialism and industrialisation, depletion has been a major concern only since the 1970s.
Wealthy nations have been described as outsourcing resource depletion to poorer nations, which suffer the greatest ecosystem losses.
The tragedy of the commons is used to explain many forms of resource depletion.

distinct_from: Fixed stock versus opportunity cost paradigm

title: Peak minerals

definition.text: A model of how the costs and impacts of mining change as ore quality declines before and after a region's mineral production peaks.

facts.text: It compares the cheap, easily reached ores mined before peak production with the costlier ores that follow.
Falling average ore grades are the key sign that production is getting more expensive, with deeper mines, more energy use and more waste rock.
Unlike coal, oil or phosphorus, most non-energy minerals and metals are unlikely to run out.

distinct_from: Fixed stock versus opportunity cost paradigm

title: Fixed stock versus opportunity cost paradigm

definition.text: A debate over whether to treat a mineral resource as a fixed physical stock, or to measure its usable amount through its price and opportunity cost.

facts.text: How best to describe resource depletion analytically is still debated.
Tilton and Lagos (2007) argued the opportunity cost view is better because price and opportunity cost represent the usable quantity.
Because total stocks and future markets are unknown, most economists do not see physical scarcity as a good guide to a resource's availability.

contested_note: Sources describe the question of how to model depletion analytically as an ongoing debate.

title: Groundwater as a non-renewable resource
article: Resource depletion#Groundwater as a non-renewable resource

definition.text: The view that much groundwater is effectively non-renewable because it refills far too slowly to be replaced within human lifetimes.

facts.text: Less than six percent of the world's water is replenished on a human timescale of 50 years.
Of the groundwater used for farming, 16–33% is non-renewable.
Overusing groundwater can lower water levels and dry up streams, harming surface ecosystems.

distinct_from: Fixed stock versus opportunity cost paradigm

definition.text: A natural resource, also called a finite resource, that nature cannot replace quickly enough to keep up with how fast people use it.

facts.text: Minerals and metal ores, fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, natural gas) and groundwater in some aquifers are all non-renewable.
Ore deposits form only where geological processes concentrate metals, which takes tens of thousands to millions of years, so near-surface deposits are non-renewable on human time-frames.
Coal, oil and gas take thousands of years to form and cannot be replaced as fast as they are used; fossil fuels are the main energy source humans use today.
Some argue carbon fuel is practically inexhaustible if methane hydrates on the sea floor are counted, though whether they can be extracted at viable cost is unknown.
In economics, a non-renewable resource is a good where using more today means less is available tomorrow.
David Ricardo argued that a mineral's price should rise over time, with the costliest mine setting the price and cheaper mines earning a differential rent.
Without regulation, people and firms tend to keep using non-renewable resources because the easier, cheaper option often differs from the environmentally friendly one.

definition.text: The idea that land can be reused but not created on demand, so economists treat it as a fixed resource whose supply cannot respond to price.

facts.text: Land surface can count as either renewable or non-renewable depending on what it is compared with.
In economic terms land has perfectly inelastic supply.
Unlike capital goods, land and non-renewable resources cannot be produced or increased.

definition.text: The question of whether nuclear fuels should count as renewable, since mined uranium is finite but breeder reactors make more fuel than they use.

facts.text: In 1987 the World Commission on Environment and Development classed breeder reactors, which produce more fissile fuel than they consume, as renewable energy sources.
Uranium, the most common fission fuel, occurs at low concentrations and is mined in 19 countries.
Nuclear power provides about 6% of the world's energy and 13–14% of its electricity.
Nuclear plants produce about 10,000 metric tons of high level waste each year worldwide, which is hazardous if not properly contained.

definition.text: A natural resource, also called a flow resource, that replaces what is used up through natural reproduction or other recurring processes within a human time scale.

facts.text: Resources whose recovery is unlikely ever to exceed a human time scale are called perpetual resources.
Water, forests, plants and animals are renewable only as long as they are adequately monitored, protected and conserved.
Water stays renewable only when its use is carefully controlled; groundwater pumped far faster than it recharges counts as non-renewable.
Sun, wind, water movement and geothermal heat are practically infinite and cannot be depleted.
Unregulated industrial growth endangers renewable resources, which must be managed so use does not exceed nature's capacity to replenish them.
Overuse of renewables such as deforestation, overgrazing and overfishing was already a large problem in early modern times.
An unregulated industry practice can lead to complete depletion of a renewable resource, as overfishing shows.
Building renewable energy devices still uses non-renewable resources such as mined metals and land.

definition.text: The branch of economics that studies the supply, demand and sharing out of the Earth's natural resources.

facts.text: A main aim is to understand nature's role in the economy so resources can be managed sustainably and stay available for future generations.
Its focus is how to run an economy within the ecological limits of the Earth's natural resources.
The traditional curriculum centred on fisheries, forestry and mineral extraction models: fish, trees and ore.
More recently air, water, the global climate and environmental resources in general have become important to policy, and interest has moved beyond optimal commercial exploitation alone.
Its traditional topics include welfare theory, land use, pollution control, resource extraction, non-market valuation, exhaustibility and sustainability.
The subfield began when researchers were mainly concerned with optimal commercial exploitation of natural resource stocks; environmental economics was once distinct from it.
Ecological economics criticises resource economics for focusing mainly on efficient allocation and less on fair distribution and the scale of the economy.

title: Stages of mineral resource development

definition.text: Vogely's five stages through which a mineral resource is developed, from the current operating margin to the technology margin.

facts.text: The five margins are the current operating margin, the intensive development margin, the extensive development margin, the exploration margin and the technology margin.
The Gray–Hotelling exhaustion theory covers only the first three stages, not the more important exploration and technology margins.

notes: Single-author scheme mentioned only on Natural resource economics; may fail curriculum tests.

title: Perpetual resource
article: Natural resource economics#Trend towards perpetual resources

definition.text: A resource so large relative to demand that it is unlikely ever to run out on a human time scale.

facts.text: Whether a resource is perpetual changes with new technology, new needs and new prices, plus how recyclable a material is and whether substitutes exist.
More efficient recovery lowers the ore grade needed: average processed copper ore fell from 4.0% copper in 1900 to 0.44% in 2000.
Salt, stone, magnesium and common clay have perpetual resources, and new technology added synthetic diamonds to the list.
Simon claimed the supply of natural resources is infinite, that is, perpetual.

title: Paleoresource
article: Natural resource economics#Transitioning: perpetual resources to paleoresources

definition.text: A resource for which there is little or no demand any more because the material taken from it has gone out of use.

facts.text: The classic example is arrowhead-grade flint, which nobody needs now that sharpened scrap steel is simpler.
US anthracite production fell from 70.4 million tonnes in 1905 to 1.5 million tonnes in 2005, so its reserves are now more than perpetual.
Decline reinforces itself: as customers switch fuels, dealers and then mines lose too much sales volume to cover costs and close.

definition.text: Replacing a scarce material with another one in its end uses, a main way economies escape shortages of a particular resource.

facts.text: Most mineral resources can be stretched by recycling and by substitutes for the end-use products.
Tin scarcity eventually led aluminium foil to replace tin foil, and polymer-lined steel cans and aseptic packaging to replace tin-plated cans.
When a 1978 invasion disrupted cobalt supply and briefly tripled its price, nickel and other substitutes were used instead.
Substitution and recycling can influence demand for minerals and so their availability.

definition.text: Any payment to the owner of a factor of production, such as land, beyond what is needed to bring that factor into use.

facts.text: Classical economists saw rent as payment for non-produced inputs such as land and location, or for privileges such as patents.
Rent is seen as unearned income, unlike economic profit, and competition cannot eliminate it.
In farming and extraction, economic rent arises from the scarcity and uneven spread of natural resources such as land, oil and minerals.
Scarcity rent is what is paid for identical land when supply is short of demand; differential rent is the surplus from better land over the poorest land in use.
Governments can collect part of resource rent as royalties or extraction fees on minerals, oil and gas.
Henry George argued that taxing unearned land rent would not distort economic activity and proposed it as the main source of public revenue.
Since the late 1800s the term has had several conflicting definitions, often used interchangeably, causing considerable confusion.
Public choice theorists later used rent for wealth transferred through state-granted rights, the source of the term rent seeking.

definition.text: A short-run, rent-like return earned by a factor of production, such as a machine or building, whose supply is fixed for the time being.

facts.text: Alfred Marshall developed the idea to extend rent reasoning from land to durable man-made factors fixed in supply in the short period.
Unlike pure rent, quasi-rent rewards the action needed to earn it, and in the long run it is competed away as new capital enters.

title: Exploitation of natural resources

definition.text: Using natural resources, often non-renewable or limited ones, to drive economic growth or development.

facts.text: It is often accompanied by environmental damage, human insecurity and social conflict.
It reached an industrial scale in the 19th century as mining, steam power and machinery expanded extraction far beyond pre-industrial levels.
Drivers include better technology, which speeds extraction, and overconsumption and consumerism, which raise demand.
Raw materials are often taken from developing countries by foreign industries, with local communities receiving little of the profit.
About 33% of the Earth's soils are moderately to highly degraded, and more than 90% could be degraded by 2050, according to the FAO.
To be sustainable, the rate at which a resource is consumed must stay equal to or below the rate at which it is supplied.
Economist Julian Simon rejected the idea that resources are finite, arguing that substitution, recycling and new technology make scarcity increasingly tenuous.

contested_note: Julian Simon and others reject the view that natural resources are fundamentally finite.

definition.text: A rule describing how the net price of a non-renewable resource should change over time when its owner extracts it so as to earn the most rent.

facts.text: With efficient extraction, the net price rises each period by a percentage equal to the discount rate, maximising the present value of the resource.

The rule implies that efficient use of a non-renewable, non-augmentable resource under stable conditions leads to its depletion, with a net price rising at the rate of interest to reflect growing scarcity.
The maximum rent obtainable while emptying the stock is called Hotelling rent or scarcity rent.
This resource rent equals the resource's net price, its selling price minus costs, and equals the shadow value of the natural capital.
Harold Hotelling published the analysis in the Journal of Political Economy in 1931; L. C. Gray had published a similar result for a single mine owner in 1914.
It is one of the best known early attempts at the economics of exhaustible resources such as fossil fuels.

conflicts.note: Natural resource economics gives 1938; Hotelling's rule and Non-renewable resource pages give 1931.

title: Peak oil

definition.text: The point when world petroleum production reaches its highest rate, after which it declines for good.

facts.text: Predictions of the peak range from 2025 to after 2050.
Reserves are finite, but the key issue is whether extraction is economically viable at current prices.
Conventional oil production is recognised to have peaked around 2005–2006; rapid growth in US tight oil since 2008 has kept total output rising.
Every oilfield eventually declines: output typically rises, plateaus and then falls, the assumption behind Hubbert peak theory.
Past predictions often failed: forecasts in 2007 and 2009 of an imminent peak were followed by record production in 2018 and 101.73 million barrels per day in 2023.
A sharp fall in oil supply could raise the costs of transport, food, heating and electricity worldwide, since modern farming depends on oil-derived fuel and chemicals.
Critics argue that as prices rise, unconventional sources become economically viable, so the world is only running out of cheap oil.

contested_note: Peak oil theory is controversial; critics argue new reserves and unconventional oil have postponed any peak.

definition.text: The idea that world oil use will peak because people deliberately reduce demand, before supply runs short.

facts.text: The International Energy Agency argues demand will be cut first to address climate change and greenhouse gas emissions.
It relies on technologies such as electric vehicles and possibly biofuels replacing gasoline and diesel vehicles.
About 50% of oil use in OECD countries is for road transport.

definition.text: The grouping of oil reserves by how likely they are to be produced: proven, probable and possible.

facts.text: 1P (proven) reserves have at least a 90% probability of production, 2P (proven and probable) at least 50%, and 3P (proven, probable and possible) at least 10%.
Conventional and unconventional reserves are counted separately.
Critics say stated world reserves are inflated, with many so-called reserves actually being resources not available for production.

definition.text: Oil that is difficult to extract, such as oil sands, as opposed to conventional oil from easy onshore and shallow offshore fields.

facts.text: The many processing steps make its production costs extremely high.
As conventional oil becomes scarcer, liquids from tight oil, oil sands, oil shale, gas-to-liquids, coal-to-liquids and biofuels can replace it.

title: Backstop resources

definition.text: The theory that as a heavily used limited resource grows expensive, alternatives become cheap by comparison and so become worth using.

facts.text: In the long run it assumes technological progress will make backstop resources essentially unlimited, with need driving new technologies to become cost effective.
Examples include Canada developing tar sands after the 1979 oil price spike and South Africa turning coal into fuel under anti-apartheid embargoes.
Critics say it ignores the infrastructure alternatives need: a hydrogen car is easy compared with building a hydrogen supply network.

contested_note: Environmental economists dispute the theory's reliance on technology and its neglect of resource exploitation and infrastructure.

title: Cornucopianism

definition.text: The view that advancing technology can keep supplying humanity's material needs, so growth is practically unlimited.

facts.text: The name comes from the cornucopia, the horn of plenty of Greek mythology; cornucopians or boomsters are contrasted with Malthusian doomsters.
Julian Simon's 1981 book The Ultimate Resource argued that humans have always found ways to develop resources past nearly any roadblock.
Simon held that free markets are needed: when a resource's price rises because supply is short, research into cheaper alternatives follows.
The label is rarely self-applied and is mostly used critically by those who see the view as over-optimistic.
Naomi Oreskes argued that many key innovations came from government action and that technological progress has not stopped the climate crisis.

contested_note: Critics such as Lindsey Grant and Naomi Oreskes reject cornucopian arguments as flawed or over-optimistic.

title: Critical raw materials

definition.text: Raw materials that have no viable substitutes with current technology, that most consuming countries must import, and whose supply is dominated by one or a few producers.

facts.text: Criticality has no agreed definition and varies with time, country and context.
The European Commission's list grew from 14 critical raw materials in 2011 to 34 in 2023; they are mainly used in energy transition and digital technologies.
In 2023 Europe relied on China for 98% of its rare-earth needs and 97% of its lithium.
The EU's Critical Raw Materials Act, in force from 23 May 2024, aims by 2030 to extract at least 10%, process at least 40% and recycle at least 25% of EU annual consumption domestically.

notes: The Critical Raw Materials Act itself is an EU law; folded in here rather than given its own entry.

definition.text: The apparent link between a boom in one sector, such as natural resources, and a decline in other sectors such as manufacturing or agriculture.

facts.text: The Economist coined the term in 1977 for the decline of Dutch manufacturing after the Groningen gas field was discovered in 1959.
Boom revenues strengthen the country's currency, making its other exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper, so those sectors lose competitiveness.
It can follow any large inflow of foreign currency, including foreign aid and foreign direct investment, not just resource discoveries.
Trade theory says resource-rich countries should specialise in extraction, but this can backfire when resources deplete, since manufacturing cannot return as fast as it left.
Remedies include saving boom revenues abroad in a sovereign wealth fund, running budget surpluses, and investing in education and infrastructure for lagging sectors.
It is hard to diagnose, but evidence suggests very large unexpected oil and gas discoveries do on average raise the real exchange rate and shrink lagging sectors.

definition.text: The classic 1982 economic model of Dutch disease, with a booming sector, a lagging tradable sector and a non-tradable services sector.

facts.text: In the resource movement effect, the boom pulls labour into the booming sector, called direct deindustrialisation.
In the spending effect, extra revenue raises demand for services, pulling labour from the lagging sector (indirect deindustrialisation) and raising the real exchange rate.
The spending effect is usually seen as the main channel, because extraction is capital-intensive and employs few workers.

definition.text: The amount of an ecosystem's growth that can be harvested while still letting it recover.

facts.text: It is most often measured in forestry, where sustainable forestry harvests no more wood in a year than grew that year in a given patch.
If more is consumed than is renewed, the ecosystem's carrying capacity shrinks over time.
It is a theoretical quantity that can only be estimated, and it depends on the recovery period chosen: three years' sustainable harvest is not necessarily three times one year's.
Firms that borrow to buy land rights may face debt that demands more yield than the land can renew, and the winner's curse leads winning bidders to overestimate it.
Only about 10% of biomass passes from prey to predator, so 100 kg of plants may yield 10 kg of herbivores and 1 kg of carnivores.
In 1986 Vitousek and colleagues estimated humans use 50 billion tons of photosynthetic biomass a year, 20% to 40% of the Earth's photosynthesis.
Measuring ecological footprints accurately requires estimating land productivity, that is, ecological yield.

definition.text: A bell-shaped curve approximating how a resource's production rate rises, peaks and falls over time.

facts.text: Geologist M. King Hubbert first presented it in 1956 to the American Petroleum Institute.
Using the 1948 peak in oil well discoveries, Hubbert predicted that oil production in the contiguous United States would peak around 1970.
It is a symmetric logistic distribution curve, often confused with the normal (Gaussian) curve, which it resembles.
Real production curves are often lopsided because of new extraction techniques, competing resources and government regulation.
US output followed the curve for 35 years after the early-1970s peak, but new extraction methods pushed it to a record 10.07 million barrels a day in November 2017.
It has been applied to natural gas, coal, uranium, copper, helium and water, and a modified version fits any resource harvested faster than it is replaced.

definition.text: The principle that the rent of a piece of land equals the extra output it produces compared with the best land available rent-free, using the same labour and capital.

facts.text: David Ricardo formulated it around 1809 and set it out fully in On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation; it is the origin of the term Ricardian rent.
In Ricardo's example, plots yield 100, 90 and 80 units of corn; once the 90-unit plot must be farmed, the best plot earns a rent of 10 units.
Ricardo argued that 'corn is not high because a rent is paid, but rent is paid because corn is high'.
The output of the best rent-free land is called the margin of production; rent is the difference between a site's productive capacity and this margin.
It applies to urban and rural land alike, and to any natural factor of production that is privately owned.
Ricardian rent differs from contract rent, the actual payments tenants make for using others' property.

title: Malthusianism

definition.text: The theory that population can grow exponentially while food and other resources grow only steadily, so living standards eventually fall until population declines.

facts.text: It stems from Thomas Robert Malthus's 1798 An Essay on the Principle of Population.
Malthus argued that technology could raise resources and living standards, but the extra abundance would fuel population growth until resources per person fell back to their old level.
A Malthusian catastrophe, or Malthusian trap, is predicted if population outpaces farm output, causing famine or war.

Evidence fits the pre-industrial era: from 1 to 1500 AD better technology raised population density but not living standards, and a labourer's daily wage bought about 15 pounds of wheat in ancient Babylonia and 13 in England in 1800.
After World War II, mechanised farming and the Green Revolution greatly raised crop yields, and most developed countries' populations grew slower than productivity.
Many models of resource depletion are Malthusian in character, predicting that consumption will outstrip new supply and cause a crisis.
Critics such as William Hazlitt argued Malthus confused natural limits on output with the artificial way society distributes it.

contested_note: Critics from Ricardo onward have disputed Malthus's theory, and 20th-century growth did not produce the predicted catastrophe.

definition.text: Malthus's two kinds of brake on population: preventive checks that lower birth rates and positive checks that shorten lives.

facts.text: Preventive checks include celibacy and chastity; positive checks are chiefly war, plague and famine, but also poor health and economic conditions.
When positive checks cause high rates of premature death, the result is called a Malthusian catastrophe.

definition.text: The concern that overpopulation and overconsumption will deplete resources and degrade the environment until ecosystems collapse.

facts.text: Post-war crop gains were followed by rapid population growth, prompting Paul R. Ehrlich and others to predict an imminent Malthusian catastrophe.
A 2004 study including Kenneth Arrow and Paul Ehrlich found that sustainability concerns had shifted from population growth to the balance between consumption and saving.
Herman Daly and Jeremy Rifkin raised neo-Malthusian concerns about modern mechanised agriculture.

sources.title: An Essay on the Principle of Population

definition.text: Physical and biological things found in the oceans that are useful to people.

facts.text: They include marine biodiversity, ecosystem services from coasts and coral reefs, minerals from deep sea mining, and marine renewable energy.
The term was popularised by Sustainable Development Goal 14, which aims to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources.
Sustainable fisheries contributed around 0.1% of global GDP per year.

definition.text: Systems for grading mineral deposits by how well they are known and whether they can be mined at a profit.

facts.text: A mineral resource is material in or on the Earth's crust with reasonable prospects for eventual economic extraction.
Resources are split, in increasing geological confidence, into inferred, indicated and measured.
A mineral reserve is the economically mineable part of a measured or indicated resource, divided into probable and, with highest confidence, proved reserves.
Most schemes follow the CRIRSCO International Reporting Template, such as Australia's JORC Code; the UN Framework Classification for Resources dates from 1997.
Ores are concentrated unevenly, so extraction eventually meets diminishing returns as it moves to less accessible sites and lower grades.

definition.text: The economic rent earned from using natural resources such as minerals, oil reserves, rivers, waterfalls, coastal space and wind.

facts.text: It is the surplus left after selling a resource's output and paying all extraction and production costs, including a normal return.
Differential (Ricardian) rent comes from better sites: a coal firm with $20/t costs earns more rent than one with $30/t costs at the same price.
Scarcity (Hotelling) rent arises because extracting a finite resource today leaves less for later; if oil's price rises from $50 to $70 while costs stay $30, rent per barrel rises from $20 to $40.
Entrepreneurial rent, or quasi-rent, comes from management skill or investment that cuts costs or raises price.
Resource rents have been called a 'natural dividend' that should belong to the people who own the resources.
In fisheries, maximum economic yield is the catch at which resource rent is greatest; catching more counts as economic overfishing.

definition.text: A tax on the rent, or surplus profit, earned by exploiting a natural resource, which can apply to renewable and non-renewable resources.

facts.text: It taxes the surplus beyond the necessary costs of production, including a reward to capital.
Investors pay nothing until they reach a set rate of return; after that, profits are shared with the host government.
It is most common in mining and petroleum; Norway has also applied it to fish farming from 2023 and onshore wind from 2024, Iceland to fishing and Switzerland to hydropower.

definition.text: A tax charged on removing natural resources such as oil, gas, coal, uranium or timber within a taxing jurisdiction.

facts.text: It is used where resources are privately owned, as in the United States; where resources are publicly owned, a resource royalty is paid instead, called stumpage in forestry.
As of 2021, 34 US states collected a severance tax on oil and gas.
Some states put the revenue into permanent endowments, from about $800 million in Montana to more than $37 billion in Alaska, meant to outlast extraction.
Severance taxes are counted among environmental taxes and cited as classic Pigouvian taxes.

title: Simon–Ehrlich wager

definition.text: A 1980 bet between economist Julian Simon and biologist Paul Ehrlich on whether natural resources would become scarcer, measured by metal prices up to 1990.

facts.text: Ehrlich, author of The Population Bomb (1968), expected resources to be outstripped by population growth; Simon bet that raw material prices would not rise in the long run.
Ehrlich chose copper, chromium, nickel, tin and tungsten, buying $200 of each on paper on 29 September 1980, with payoff on 29 September 1990.
All five fell in inflation-adjusted price even though world population grew by more than 800 million, and Ehrlich paid Simon $576.07.
Over 1980–2011 Simon would have lost on four of the five metals, and one study found he would have won in only 38.4% of periods from 1900 to 2008.
Some analysts conclude the bet shows luck mattered more than expertise, and does not prove there are no environmental limits to growth.
Simon declined Ehrlich and Schneider's later offer to bet on 15 environmental trends; he would have lost on 11 of them.

contested_note: Observers disagree on what the wager proves, since the result depends heavily on the time period chosen.

definition.text: A state-owned investment fund that invests in assets such as stocks, bonds, real estate and precious metals.

facts.text: Most are funded by commodity export revenues or by central bank foreign exchange reserves, and many were set up by oil-rich states.
For commodity-exporting countries, a fund can smooth volatile government revenue and save for the longer term.
The first for a sovereign state was the Kuwait Investment Authority, created from oil revenues in 1953.
Assets under management reached $13–15 trillion by 2025; funds built on oil and gas exports held $5.4 trillion as of 2020.
The 24 Santiago Principles, drafted in 2008 under IMF leadership, set standards for transparency, independence and accountability.
Many funds have been exhausted, mainly because of political instability rather than economic factors.

definition.text: The amount of a renewable resource people can harvest without over-harvesting or damaging it.

facts.text: Formally, it is the ecological yield that can be taken without shrinking the natural capital itself, keeping ecosystem services at the same level or higher.
It applies only to renewable resources, since extracting non-renewable resources always reduces natural capital.
It is often calculated as half the carrying capacity, the population level at which a stock can be harvested and still regrow.
It changes over time: a forest hit by a natural disaster needs more of its own yield to recover, so its sustainable yield falls.
It is used mostly in forestry, fisheries and groundwater, where a 'safe yield' marks the extraction rate beyond which an aquifer is overdrawn.
Overfishing in the mid-1850s led to maximum sustainable yield becoming a reference point for fishery management.
Sustainable yield forestry is criticised for focusing only on wood, changing landscapes and reducing biodiversity; the term has also been called anthropocentric.
In fisheries, fishing shrinks the original population while breeding and growth add to it; sustainable yield is the balance between the two.

conflicts.text: Under the logistic model, maximum sustainable yield is at exactly half the carrying capacity.
conflicts.note: Different model assumptions (logistic vs modern age-structured models), noted for the verifier; not strictly the same definition.

definition.text: Economic use of oceans, lakes, rivers and coasts, generally with an emphasis on using their resources sustainably.

facts.text: There is no agreed definition; the World Bank calls it sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, livelihoods and jobs while preserving ocean ecosystem health.
It spans fisheries, aquaculture, shipping and tourism as well as emerging activities such as offshore renewable energy, blue carbon and seabed mining.
It also covers unpriced ocean ecosystem services such as carbon sequestration, coastal protection and biodiversity.
The term was popularised by the Rio+20 UN Conference on Sustainable Development in 2012.
Mangrove forests support more than 4 million fishers and protect coasts, yet 0.5% have been lost each year on average since the 2000s.
In 2023 the EU's blue economy employed nearly 4.9 million people and added €263 billion in gross value added.
Misleading claims about effects on aquatic environments have been called bluewashing, by analogy with greenwashing.

definition.text: Finance that cuts the carbon footprint of ocean-related activities and benefits the marine environment, as part of sustainable finance.

facts.text: The World Economic Forum estimates US$175 billion a year is needed to meet SDG 14, the most underfunded of the 17 goals.
It funds marine renewable energy, zero-emissions shipping and restoration of mangroves and seagrass meadows.
It is part of sustainable finance and overlaps with climate finance, funding offshore wind, zero-emission shipping and the restoration of mangroves and seagrass.
The World Economic Forum says US$175 billion a year is needed to reach SDG 14, the most underfunded of the 17 SDGs.

definition.text: A critical approach examining how blue economy and blue growth initiatives affect coastal communities and small-scale fisheries.

facts.text: It recognises small-scale fishing communities' historical rights to marine resources and coastal space, sometimes used for thousands of years.
It studies pressures on these fisheries from industrial fishing, tourism, aquaculture and energy production.

definition.text: Something drawn from nature and used with few changes, such as sunlight, air, water, land, minerals, plants and wildlife.

facts.text: Every man-made product is made, at bottom, from natural resources.
Some resources are renewable and are restored by natural processes, while many extractive industries rely on non-renewable resources that can be extracted only once.
Who gets natural resources is at the centre of many economic and political confrontations, especially when scarcity is increasing.
Resource extraction is a major source of human rights violations and environmental damage.
In 1982 the UN's World Charter for Nature recognised the need to protect nature from further depletion by human activity.
Natural resource management focuses on how managing land, water, soil, plants and animals affects quality of life for present and future generations.

definition.text: Ways of sorting natural resources by origin, stage of development, renewability and ownership.

facts.text: By origin, resources are biotic, from living things (including fossil fuels formed from decayed organic matter), or abiotic, from non-living material such as land, water and ores.
By stage of development, potential resources are known but unused, such as unextracted petroleum, while actual resources are surveyed and in use.
By ownership, resources can be individual, community, national or international, such as international waters.

definition.text: A war caused by conflict over resources, typically between whoever controls a resource and an aggressor who wants it.

facts.text: Industrialisation raised the raw materials nations need, and such power struggles have underlain conflicts since the late 19th century.
A classic example is the 19th-century conflict over guano, a nutrient-rich fertiliser, on Peru's Chincha Islands.
The geopolitical view sees resource conflict as strategic; the environmental security view sees it as a response to scarcity.
Conflicts can occur over control of resources and their revenues, one of the arguments linking resources with war.

definition.text: Natural resources extracted in a conflict zone and sold to keep the fighting going.

facts.text: The idea emerged in the late 1990s with 'blood diamonds' that financed rebellions in Angola and Sierra Leone, followed by 'conflict timber' in Cambodia and Liberia.
There is statistical and anecdotal evidence that precious commodities can prolong conflicts.
The US, EU and OECD treat tantalum, tin, tungsten and gold linked to conflict in the DRC as conflict minerals and require companies to report their use.

definition.text: The scarcity rent on a finite resource: the extra value it earns because extracting it today leaves less for the future.

facts.text: It is the maximum rent obtainable while emptying the resource stock, also called scarcity or depletion rent.
Under Hotelling's rule it rises each year at the rate of interest, reflecting growing scarcity.
It reflects choice over time: if today's price were lower, a producer would rather extract less now and more later.
Scarcity rents help explain why the best tax on a pollutant from a finite fuel can be lower than the pollutant's marginal damages.

definition.text: The tendency for extraction to become costlier as a resource stock is drawn down, pushing producers to less accessible sites and lower-grade ores.

facts.text: Because ores are concentrated unevenly, mining eventually meets diminishing returns, and extraction costs and prices of extra output tend to rise over time.
Falling average ore grades mean deeper mines, more energy use and more waste rock.
Even with constant extraction costs, a resource's value rises as it grows scarcer.

definition.text: Measures, such as a resource's inflation-adjusted price, used to judge whether natural resources are becoming scarcer.

facts.text: Because total stocks and future markets are unknown, most economists do not see physical scarcity as a good indicator of availability.
An alternative view measures the usable quantity of a resource through its price and opportunity cost.
The Simon–Ehrlich wager used the inflation-adjusted prices of five metals as its agreed measure of scarcity.
From 2005 through 2013, real prices of energy and metals stayed well above their long-term averages.
